source.title_on_document: Emergent Learner Agency in Implicit Human–AI Collaboration: How Supportive and Contrarian AI Personas Reshape Interaction

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplement. Appendix A (task text) and Appendix B (persona prompts) are in this PDF, pp. 28-30. Data available from the corresponding author on request (p. 23).

paper_design_summary: 224 university students recruited via Prolific were randomized at the triad level to 97 online triads: human-only control (30 groups of three humans), or two humans plus an undisclosed GPT-5 teammate with a supportive persona (33 groups) or a contrarian persona (34 groups). Each student wrote an individual movie-plot synopsis, took part in a 10-minute group chat to build a story outline, then wrote a revised individual synopsis without AI or chat access. Creative performance is the change in Divergent Semantic Integration (DSI) between the two individual synopses; the paper also analyzes chat discourse and self-reported cognitive load, teamwork satisfaction, and psychological safety.

arms.name: Human-only Control
arms.description: 30 groups of three human participants; no AI.

arms.name: Supportive-AI

participants.exclusions: No exclusions reported. 224 human speakers appear in the clustering analysis (p. 18, '291 speakers were identified (224 human, 67 AI)'). The sample size of the regression and Kruskal-Wallis analyses of creative performance is not stated. Per-arm people counts are not printed; group counts and composition imply 90 / 66 / 68 (computed, not printed).
participants.who: University students (50.7% female) recruited via Prolific for an online small-group collaboration study.
participants.quote: A total of 224 university students (50.7% female) were recruited via Prolific to take part in an online small-group collaboration study.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-5-based generative models (persona prompts in Appendix B)
ai_tool.how_used: An undisclosed AI teammate took part in the 10-minute group text chat as if it were a human student, posting with a probabilistic schedule (about every 25 seconds, 50 percent probability, at most three consecutive turns). Participants were told they would work with 'two other online students'. Detection in the manipulation check was 25.5% (Supportive) and 31.6% (Contrarian). AI was not available during the individual post-task writing.

task.description: Write a sci-fi movie plot that begins 'In the year 2045, the world's first AGI unexpectedly...'. Individual baseline synopsis (50-100 words), then a group chat to jointly build a story outline, then an individual revised synopsis written without access to the baseline or the chat log.
task.duration: 10-minute group discussion; durations of the individual writing phases not stated

outcomes.name: Creative performance change (Divergent Semantic Integration, post minus pre)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Divergent Semantic Integration (DSI; Johnson et al., 2023), an embedding-based metric of semantic expansiveness of short creative texts, computed on each participant's 50-100 word synopsis before and after the group discussion; DSI scores standardized and differenced into a change score (p. 10). In the OLS models outcomes were rescaled to [0, 1] and HC3 robust SEs used; group-clustered SEs reported as substantively identical (p. 13).
outcomes.delay: Post-task synopsis written right after the 10-minute discussion, same session.

contrasts.reported: Kruskal-Wallis omnibus across three conditions: 'condition did not significantly affect ... creative performance gains (all p > .05)'. OLS Q(Outcome) ~ C(cluster) + C(condition): 'creative performance gains ... were not predicted by either cluster or condition (F = 1.20, p = .310, R2 = .029)'. No arm means, SDs, or condition coefficients printed.
Same omnibus results: Kruskal-Wallis 'all p > .05'; OLS F = 1.20, p = .310, R2 = .029. No arm-specific estimates printed.
Same omnibus results: Kruskal-Wallis 'all p > .05'; OLS F = 1.20, p = .310, R2 = .029. No pairwise estimates printed.

company_involvement.description: Academic authors (Monash, Hong Kong, Tsinghua); funding from NSFC, Australian Research Council, and Jacobs Foundation; no conflicts declared. The AI teammate was GPT-5-based.

eligibility.reason: Triads (97) were randomized to include an undisclosed GPT-5 teammate (supportive or contrarian) or to be human-only, on a creative story task (p. 7). 224 students took part (p. 7, p. 18). The individual post-discussion synopsis is scored with DSI, an automated creativity measure (p. 10), and was written after AI was removed, so the outcome answers after_ai. Caveats: the AI acted as a covert teammate, not an assistant the person used; randomization was by triad (97 clusters); the control replaces the AI with a third human, so the AI-vs-control contrast is coded ai_vs_active; only omnibus F and p are printed for creativity.

one_line_finding: Neither a supportive nor a contrarian undisclosed AI teammate changed students' individual post-discussion creative performance (DSI change): Kruskal-Wallis all p > .05 (p. 18) and OLS F = 1.20, p = .310, R2 = .029 (p. 19).

notes: Outcomes not listed because they are not scored on output: self-reported intrinsic, germane, and extraneous cognitive load, teamwork satisfaction, and psychological safety (Table 2, p. 10; results pp. 18-19). Discourse-process outcomes (transition network edges, sequential motifs, GMM agency clusters; pp. 13-18) describe chat moves, not creativity of the output. The jointly built group story outline was not scored. Pilot test (N = 15) rated AI human-likeness M = 5.43 (p. 9).
